title: The Pipeline Mirage

scenario.situation: Qualified leads are up 40% this quarter, but revenue is flat — and leadership is pointing fingers at the sales team.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The VP of Sales believes the SDR team is finally delivering quality leads, and that account executives are fumbling the handoff and losing deals.
scenario.question: Is the sales team really underperforming, or is something else going on?

decisions.prompt: Leadership wants answers fast. How do you structure the investigation?

options.label: Audit AE activity on the new leads
options.detail: Pull call logs, email cadences, and CRM touchpoints for AEs handling leads from this quarter.
options.consequence: You find normal activity levels — AEs look fine. But you've spent a week investigating the symptom leadership pointed at, not the actual data structure. The real question was never asked.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the blame narrative and investigated people instead of the pipeline mechanics.

options.label: Map the full revenue lifecycle
options.detail: Trace a cohort of leads from entry through close, measuring how long each stage takes and which input period actually feeds this quarter's revenue.
options.consequence: You discover the median lead-to-close time is roughly six months. This quarter's revenue can't possibly reflect this quarter's leads — they haven't had time to close. The whole comparison is a time-window mismatch.

options.label: Compare win rates this quarter vs. last
options.detail: Calculate the percentage of leads that converted to closed-won deals in each quarter.
options.consequence: Win rates look roughly unchanged, but the calculation quietly mixes lead cohorts from different periods with revenue from the current period. You've measured the mismatch without noticing it.
options.divergenceCost: Used a metric that inherited the time-window mismatch rather than diagnosing it.

options.label: Segment leads by source to find quality issues
options.detail: Break down the 40% lead increase by channel to check if new leads are lower quality.
options.consequence: Lead quality looks acceptable across channels. You've ruled out one hypothesis but still haven't explained why flat revenue and rising leads coexist — the core question is unanswered.
options.divergenceCost: Chased a quality hypothesis and left the timing structure unexamined.

decisions.prompt: You suspect timing is the issue. Which metric do you use to test it?

artifact.title: Leads generated vs. Revenue closed — by current quarter
artifact.caption: Raw leads and revenue plotted in the same quarter. The gap this quarter looks damning — but is the comparison valid?

options.label: Leads generated vs. revenue closed in the same quarter
options.detail: Plot this quarter's lead volume against this quarter's closed revenue, as leadership has been doing.
options.consequence: The chart makes it look like the sales team is leaving money on the table — lots of leads, flat revenue. But you're comparing inputs from today to outputs that were seeded six months ago. The metric is measuring nothing real.
options.divergenceCost: Reproduced the exact apples-to-oranges comparison that created the false alarm.

options.label: Revenue closed in a quarter vs. leads generated two quarters prior (lag-adjusted)
options.detail: Shift the lead series back by the observed ~6-month median sales cycle and replot the relationship.
options.consequence: Once you align the series by the lag, the relationship snaps into place: this quarter's revenue tracks cleanly with leads from two quarters ago — which were lower. The sales team's close rate is normal. The pipeline is healthy; it just hasn't matured yet.

artifact.title: Revenue closed (this Q) vs. Leads generated 2 quarters prior (lag-adjusted)

bars.label: Leads gen. Q-2 (fed this Q revenue)
Leads gen. this Q (will feed Q+2)

artifact.caption: Lag-adjusted view: current revenue aligns tightly with the smaller lead cohort from two quarters ago. The 40% lead surge will show up in revenue — in two quarters.

decisions.prompt: The lag-adjusted view shows the pipeline is healthy and a revenue lift is likely in two quarters. What do you tell leadership?

options.label: "Sales is fine — revenue will jump 40% in two quarters. Stand down."
options.detail: Declare the problem solved and project the outcome confidently.
options.consequence: You've made a precise forward forecast from a single observed lag, assuming nothing else changes — close rate, deal size, or churn in the pipeline. If any of those shift, you've overcredentialed a projection and eroded your credibility.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed a precise future outcome from a structural observation alone.

options.label: "The comparison was misaligned by ~6 months; the lag-adjusted view shows normal close rates. We should track the current lead cohort through the pipeline before drawing conclusions about performance."
options.detail: Present the finding, flag the time-window error, and recommend monitoring the cohort forward.
options.consequence: Leadership updates their mental model of how leading and lagging indicators connect. The sales team is no longer under a false spotlight. You've proposed a concrete next step — cohort tracking — that will surface real performance signals as the new leads mature.

insight: The 'pipeline mirage' wasn't a sales execution problem — it was a time-window mismatch. Today's revenue reflects leads from two quarters ago, not today's, because the sales cycle is ~six months long. Plotting a leading indicator and a lagging indicator in the same time window creates a spurious gap that looks like underperformance. The core lesson: before comparing any two metrics, ask whether their reference periods are actually aligned to the same underlying cohort.
